parts.title: Passage 1
parts.content:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Urban Green Infrastructure and Climate Resilience

A. As metropolitan regions worldwide grapple with intensifying heatwaves and extreme precipitation events driven by global climate change, urban planners and environmental engineers are increasingly turning away from traditional hard-engineering solutions in favour of nature-based strategies. Urban green infrastructure—the strategically planned network of natural and semi-natural areas designed and managed to deliver a wide range of ecosystem services—is emerging as a cornerstone of sustainable city development. By integrating vegetation, soils, and natural hydrological cycles directly into urban fabrics, cities can bolster their resilience against environmental shocks while enhancing public health and livability.

B. One of the most acute challenges confronting modern cities is the urban heat island effect, a meteorological phenomenon whereby built environments experience substantially higher ambient temperatures than surrounding rural landscapes. This discrepancy arises primarily because conventional construction materials like asphalt and concrete absorb and re-radiate vast amounts of solar radiation, while human activities generate massive volumes of waste heat. Urban tree canopies counteract this thermal loading through two complementary mechanisms: physical shading and evapotranspiration. Trees intercept incoming sunlight before it reaches ground surfaces, preventing heat storage. Simultaneously, plant roots draw moisture from the soil and release water vapour into the atmosphere through microscopic leaf pores, consuming thermal energy in the process and cooling local air temperatures by up to several degrees Celsius.

C. In addition to thermal regulation, urban green infrastructure plays a pivotal role in sustainable stormwater management. In conventional cities dominated by impervious surfaces, rainfall cannot infiltrate the ground naturally. Instead, it generates rapid surface runoff that overwhelms municipal drainage networks, leading to severe flash flooding and discharging untreated pollutants directly into local waterways. Nature-based stormwater interventions, such as bioswales, rain gardens, and engineered retention ponds, mimic natural hydrological systems by slowing down water movement, encouraging ground infiltration, and trapping particulate contaminants through soil filtration and biological uptake by wetland plants.

D. Green roofs—vegetated layers planted over waterproofing membranes on building rooftops—represent another highly effective component of green infrastructure. In addition to intercepting up to seventy percent of seasonal precipitation, green roofs provide substantial thermal insulation, reducing the energy required for mechanical cooling during summer months and retaining interior heat in winter. Furthermore, extensive green roof networks serve as vital biodiversity stepping stones, providing refuge and foraging habitats for pollinators, songbirds, and beneficial insects in densely built urban cores where ground-level parkland is scarce.

E. Despite these established benefits, the widespread deployment of green infrastructure encounters notable institutional and economic obstacles. Municipal governments frequently face tight municipal budgets, where the upfront capital expenditure of retrofitting existing streets with vegetated swales or permeable pavements competes with other essential public services. Moreover, green assets require ongoing maintenance, such as irrigation, pruning, and debris removal, which traditional public works departments may lack the staffing or horticultural expertise to manage effectively. Nonetheless, comprehensive life-cycle cost analyses consistently indicate that the long-term economic dividends of green infrastructure—manifested in averted flood damages, reduced healthcare costs, lower energy bills, and elevated property values—far exceed initial implementation expenditures.

parts.title: Passage 2
parts.content:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

The Cognitive Psychology of Deep Reading and Digital Media

A. Human beings were never biologically born to read. While spoken language is hardwired into our evolutionary biology through innate neural structures that develop automatically in early childhood, literacy requires an unnatural cognitive invention. To read, the human brain must repurpose and weave together disparate neural circuits initially evolved for vision, motor coordination, and spoken language. Because reading is a culturally acquired skill, the neurological architecture of the reading brain is fundamentally plastic—it adapts dynamically to the physical characteristics of the medium through which text is consumed.

B. Over the past two decades, the global shift from printed paper to digital screens has sparked intensive investigation among cognitive psychologists, neuroscientists, and educators. Cognitive scientist Maryanne Wolf cautions that the constant consumption of fragmented digital text is subtly transforming how our brains process written information. On digital devices, reading often devolves into skimming, rapid word-spotting, and scrolling, driven by the brain's desire to extract quick information amidst visual distractions. Eye-tracking experiments demonstrate that screen readers rarely read sequentially; instead, their gaze darts across the page in an 'F-shaped' pattern, absorbing headlines and initial sentences while skipping dense paragraphs.

C. This reading style exerts profound implications for what cognitive theorists call 'deep reading' processes. Deep reading encompasses sophisticated intellectual operations, including inductive reasoning, critical analysis, analogical thinking, and empathetic identification with characters or authors. Technology critic Nicholas Carr argues that the cognitive overload induced by hyperlinks, push notifications, and visual stimuli fragments our working memory, preventing information from transitioning into deep long-term memory stores. Without the quiet mental space required for contemplation, readers risk becoming mere decoders of information rather than thoughtful evaluators of meaning.

D. Empirical studies corroborate these concerns. In controlled trials conducted by linguist Naomi Baron, university students who read complex expository texts in print consistently demonstrated superior comprehension and recall compared to peers who read identical material on digital screens. Printed text provides tactile and spatial landmarks—such as the physical thickness of pages turned and fixed topography of text on a page—that construct a coherent cognitive map in the reader's mind. Conversely, digital scrolling disrupts this spatial anchoring, causing mental fatigue and reducing narrative retention.

E. However, cognitive scientists do not advocate abandoning digital technology. Instead, educational researcher Anne Mangen proposes cultivating a 'bi-literate' brain. Under this paradigm, children are taught to master both modes of literacy deliberately: agile digital skimming for rapid research and information gathering, alongside sustained, uninterrupted immersion in printed text for deep intellectual reflection and empathetic growth. By understanding how the reading medium shapes cognition, societies can preserve the deep contemplative mind while harnessing the immense advantages of the digital era.

Write the correct number, i–viii, in boxes 27–31 on your answer sheet.

List of Headings

ii Early philosophical concepts and the formal definition of biomimicry

iii Architectural climate control modeled on insect nests

iv The future of synthetic food production

v Hydrodynamic and antibacterial surfaces inspired by marine predators

vi Botanical and reptilian models for self-cleaning and adhesive surfaces

vii The evolutionary failure of human inventions

viii Structural materials inspired by avian bone density

28. Section B ....................

29. Section C ....................

30. Section D ....................

Biomimicry: Engineering Inspired by Nature

A. For nearly four billion years, biological organisms have undergone relentless testing and refinement in nature's vast laboratory of natural selection. Every creature surviving today embodies elegant, energy-efficient solutions to complex physical, chemical, and structural challenges. The practice of emulating biological models, systems, and processes to solve human engineering problems is known as biomimicry—a term coined by American biophysicist Otto Schmitt in the mid-twentieth century and later popularized by science writer Janine Benyus. While early thinkers such as Leonardo da Vinci sketched flying apparatuses inspired by avian flight, modern biomimicry utilizes advanced electron microscopy and nanotechnology to decode nature's microscopic blueprints.

B. One of the most famous applications of biomimicry occurred in the Japanese railway network during the 1990s. When engineers tested the original Shinkansen 500-Series bullet train, the high-speed locomotive generated severe noise pollution. As the train entered narrow tunnels at speeds exceeding 300 kilometres per hour, sudden changes in atmospheric air pressure created an explosive shockwave known as a sonic boom, rattling windows and disturbing residents for kilometres around. Eiji Nakatsu, the chief engineer and an avid birdwatcher, realized that the kingfisher provided a natural solution. Kingfishers dive from air into water—a medium eight hundred times denser—with scarcely a splash. By redesigning the train's front nose cone to resemble the streamlined, tapered beak of a kingfisher, engineers eliminated the tunnel sonic boom, reduced electricity consumption by fifteen percent, and increased operating speeds.

C. In civil architecture, biomimicry has revolutionized passive thermal climate control. When architect Mick Pearce was tasked with designing the Eastgate Centre, a major office and shopping complex in Harare, Zimbabwe, he sought to eliminate energy-intensive conventional air conditioning. Pearce turned to the architectural marvels of macrotermes bellicosus, a local species of termite. These insects construct towering termite mounds that maintain an interior temperature of exactly thirty degrees Celsius year-round, despite extreme outdoor temperatures fluctuating between zero and forty degrees. Pearce copied the termite mound's ventilation system, designing a building with hollow floors, chimneys, and dynamic airflow flues that passively draw cool air from the basement during the night and vent warm air out through roof shafts during the day, using ninety percent less energy than conventional office buildings.

D. In the marine and transport sectors, sharkskin has inspired breakthrough hydrodynamic surfaces. Despite swimming slowly through microbe-rich waters, sharks remain strikingly clean, free of algae and barnacles. Marine biologists discovered that shark skin is covered with microscopic ribbed scales known as dermal denticles. These microscopic grooves disrupt the formation of turbulent water vortices along the shark's body, drastically reducing drag while creating an inhospitable surface where bacteria cannot easily attach. Synthetic riblet films mimicking sharkskin are now applied to commercial airliner hulls to curb fuel burn, as well as hospital wall coatings to impede bacterial transmission without antibiotics.

E. Further remarkable discoveries have emerged from botanical and reptilian investigations. The leaves of the sacred lotus flower exhibit remarkable water repellency and self-cleaning traits: microscopic wax crystals cause water droplets to bead into perfect spheres that roll off the leaf, carrying dirt and fungal spores with them. This 'lotus effect' has inspired hydrophobic exterior paints and stain-resistant window glass. Similarly, the ability of geckos to run effortlessly up sheer vertical glass walls stems from millions of microscopic hairs called setae on their toes, which generate molecular van der Waals forces of dry adhesion. By replicating these microscopic setae, materials scientists have developed reusable adhesives capable of functioning in outer space.
